1149.title: The first three petitions (CCC 2803–2827)
1149.hook: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will
1149.howItsDone: Catholics pray these three petitions every time they say the Our Father, at Mass, in the rosary and at home; some pause on 'thy will be done' when facing a hard decision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole gospel in a prayer: Tertullian's short summary, the Our Father. Your line was the whole gospel.

A wedding reception. The best man taps a glass, and for the whole first part of his speech he doesn't mention himself once. It's all about the couple: who they are, what they're building, what he hopes for them. Only near the end does he get to himself, and even then it's mostly a thank-you. Nobody finds that strange. That's how speaking about someone you love tends to go. The Catechism notices the Our Father is built the same way. Before a single request for ourselves, three lines in a row turn toward God. Today: the first three petitions.
screen: `A TOAST AT A WEDDING.` → `THE COUPLE FIRST.` → `THREE LINES TURN TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Listen to the little word that repeats, in the Douay-Rheims: "hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Thy, thy, thy. The Catechism counts seven petitions, and says these first three draw us toward the Father's glory, for his own sake. It is the way of love, it says, to think first of the one we love. Thy name. To hallow means to hold as holy. We don't make God holy by saying it; God's name already is. We ask that it be recognized as holy, and kept holy in us, in how we live. Thy kingdom. Jesus began preaching with the kingdom at hand. This petition looks first to the final coming of God's reign when Christ returns, and also to that kingdom growing now, quietly, wherever people live by the Spirit. Thy will. Here the prayer meets Gethsemane. On the night of his arrest Jesus prays, "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." He asks for what he wants. Then he hands it over. And what is that will? The Catechism points to Paul: God "will have all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth." So the first half of the Our Father isn't small talk before the real requests. In the Catholic reading, it reorders everything that comes after.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want right now, honestly, the way Jesus did in the garden, and say it plainly inside. If you pray, add his words, "not my will, but thine be done," and leave a long silence after them; if you don't, loosen your grip on it a little, the way you'd open a closed hand.
The first three petitions. In the Our Father: hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, the requests that turn toward God first, for his own sake.
Your line: thy, thy, thy. Love speaks of the one it loves first. See you tomorrow.

1150.title: The last four petitions (CCC 2828–2854)
1150.howItsDone: Catholics pray these petitions in every Our Father; at Mass it is said just before Communion, and some hear 'our daily bread' there as pointing to the Eucharist as well as ordinary food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first three petitions: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will. Your line was thy, thy, thy.

The Douay-Rheims Bible gives the same bread two different names. In Luke, the Our Father asks, "Give us this day our daily bread." Turn back to Matthew, same prayer, and it reads, "Give us this day our supersubstantial bread." Supersubstantial. Nobody says that at the bakery. It isn't a typo, and it isn't careless. It sits right on a real puzzle in the prayer, and the Catechism walks straight into it. The prayer has turned toward God three times. Now it turns toward us. Today: the last four petitions.
screen: `DAILY BREAD, IN LUKE.` → `SUPERSUBSTANTIAL, IN MATTHEW.` → `NOW THE PRAYER TURNS TO US.`

segments.voice: Give. The Catechism notes that the Greek word behind daily, epiousios, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Read one way, it points to time: bread for this day, enough for now. Read more literally, it points beyond ordinary bread, to the bread of life, which Catholics understand as Christ himself in the Eucharist. The Church keeps both: bread for the table, and bread for the soul. Forgive. "And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." The Catechism calls this petition astonishing, and leans on the small word as. God's mercy can't get into a heart that refuses to forgive. Not because the mercy is small, but because a closed heart is closed. Lead. "And lead us not into temptation." Does God lead anyone into temptation? The letter of James answers flatly: "God is not a tempter of evils, and he tempteth no man." The Catechism says the Greek carries two shades: don't let us enter into temptation, and don't let us give in to it. Deliver. "But deliver us from evil." Here, the Catechism says, evil isn't only an idea. It names a person, the evil one, who opposes God, and reads the petition as asking to be freed from all evil, past, present and future, of which he is the author. Give, forgive, lead, deliver. Four requests, all plural. Us, not me.

segments.voice: Ask yourself what you actually need for today, not this year, just today: food, maybe, or patience, or one honest conversation, or rest. Then think of one other person who needs bread today, of any kind. If you pray, say "Give us this day our daily bread" with both of you in the us; if you don't, hold the two needs side by side.
The last four petitions. In the Our Father: give us bread, forgive us as we forgive, lead us not into temptation, deliver us from evil.

1151.title: The final Amen (CCC 2855–2865)
1151.hook: the Catechism ends where prayer ends: Amen
1151.howItsDone: Catholics end their prayers with Amen and answer Amen many times during Mass, including when receiving Communion; at Mass, the Our Father is followed by a short prayer of the priest and then the people's words of praise to God's kingdom, power and glory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last four petitions: bread, forgiveness, temptation, deliverance. Your line was give, forgive, lead, deliver.

A thick book on a table. It holds the creed line by line, the sacraments one by one, the commandments, and then a long walk through prayer. Turn to its very last paragraph, and what it's talking about is one small word. Not a doctrine. Not a rule. A word said at the end of prayers, often without a thought. The Catechism of the Catholic Church closes on Amen. We've read it part by part since the start of this year, and today we reach that same last word. Today: the final Amen.
screen: `A THICK BOOK.` → `ITS LAST PARAGRAPH.` → `ONE SMALL WORD.`

segments.voice: First, what comes just before it. In the Douay-Rheims, Matthew's Our Father ends simply: "But deliver us from evil. Amen." Christians who use the King James wording go on: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever." At Mass, Catholics say words of praise much like these, after a short prayer by the priest. The Catechism says this praise gathers up the first three petitions, the name, the kingdom, the will, and hands them back to God. Then the Amen, which you met at Mass back on day one hundred fifteen. The Catechism quotes Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching new Christians: after the prayer, you say Amen, which means so be it, and so put your seal on everything the prayer contains. A signature at the bottom of a letter. In its final paragraph the Catechism goes one step further: the last Amen is our own yes to all seven petitions. Days ago we met Mary's yes at the angel's word. Here everyone who prays gets to say one like it. And in Revelation, Christ himself is given the name: "These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness." So for Catholics the word that ends the prayer is also a name for the one it goes through. Now look back. The Catechism has four parts, and we've walked them all this year: what the Church believes, how it celebrates, how it lives, how it prays. It ends with a word a small child can say.
screen: `THINE IS THE KINGDOM.` · `AMEN: SO BE IT, A SEAL.` · `OUR YES TO EVERY PETITION.` · `FOUR PARTS, ONE LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one line of the Our Father you most want to mean today, say it, and answer it with one deliberate Amen, like a signature; take another line if there's time. If you don't pray, think back over these months, one belief, one sacrament, one way of living, one prayer that stayed with you, and let them rest together.

1152.title: The boy in the tower
1152.hook: his noble family locks him up to stop him becoming a Dominican
1152.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Thomas Aquinas each year, and Dominicans and Catholic schools often tell the story of his confinement when they speak about holding to a vocation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the final Amen, where our long walk through the Catechism ended. Your line was amen.

A young friar walks the road in the white habit of a new preaching order. Then horsemen. His own brothers, soldiers, ride him down, the old lives say, and carry him home to the family castle. His family were nobles with a plan for him: a respectable post in the Church, near home, with standing and land. Not a begging friar who owned nothing and preached wherever people would listen. So they shut him in, and waited for him to change his mind. His name was Thomas Aquinas. A new block begins with him, in a locked room.
screen: `A FRIAR ON THE ROAD.` → `HIS BROTHERS RIDE HIM DOWN.` → `SHUT IN AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the confinement lasted a long time, by some tellings a year or more. His mother wanted her son back; his brothers wanted the habit gone. Thomas stayed put, and stayed a Dominican. He used the time. The old accounts say he read the Scriptures, studied Peter Lombard's book of theology, the Sentences, and taught his sisters. Tradition says one sister was so moved that she later gave her own life to God as a nun. Then the hard scene, told plainly. The brothers, the story goes, sent a woman into his room to pull him away from his vows. Thomas grabbed a burning stick from the fire, drove her out, and marked a cross on the wall with it. Tradition adds that he prayed, fell asleep, and dreamed of angels binding a cord around his waist, and was not troubled that way again. In the end the family gave up. One telling has him let down from a window in a basket, back to his brothers in the order. The Summa, the long, careful book ahead, was written by a man who first had to decide what he was for. His family's plan wasn't wicked. It was sensible, even generous. His call was quieter and poorer. In Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Catholics honor Thomas as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. Before the arguments, there was a door he wouldn't let anyone close.

1153.title: How the Summa works
1153.hook: objections first, then on the contrary, then I answer that, then replies
1153.howItsDone: Catholic seminaries and universities often teach students to read an article of the Summa in its four moves, objections, on the contrary, I answer that, and replies, and some use the same shape for classroom debates.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy in the tower, who came out still a Dominican. Your line was he kept his call.

It seems that God does not exist. That sentence sits in the Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas, a friar and a saint who gave his life to God. He wrote it on purpose, then gave the reasons someone might say it. If God were infinite goodness, there would be no evil, and there is evil. And nature seems able to explain itself without any God. He set out the case against his own faith, plainly, before one word in reply. That's the method, article after article. Today's word is the book built that way.
screen: `IT SEEMS THAT GOD DOES NOT EXIST.` → `WRITTEN BY A SAINT.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The Summa Theologiae is Thomas's great book of theology, and its opening lines say who it's for: beginners. So it's built to be followed one small step at a time. It's cut into questions, and each question into articles. Every article asks one thing, as a yes or no. Whether God exists. Whether God is good. And every article moves the same way. First, the objections. Each opens, it seems that, and gives the strongest reasons for the answer Thomas won't finally take. He states the other side the way its friends would. Second, on the contrary: usually one short line from a voice the Church trusts, often Scripture, sometimes an earlier teacher like Augustine. A signal that there's another side to weigh. Third, I answer that. Now Thomas speaks for himself and gives his reasons, in order. Fourth, the replies. He goes back to the objections one by one, often granting what's true in each before showing where it goes wrong. Nothing raised at the start is left hanging. Some readers hear in this the debates of the medieval schools, written down. But notice what the shape asks of the writer. You can't answer an objection you've never really heard. You have to say it well enough that the person who holds it would say, yes, that's what I mean. The first letter of Peter gives the reason, in the Douay-Rheims: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." Ready, and listening first.
screen: `OBJECTIONS: IT SEEMS THAT…` · `ON THE CONTRARY` · `I ANSWER THAT` · `REPLIES, ONE BY ONE` · then, large: `A REASON OF THAT HOPE WHICH IS IN YOU.`

1154.title: Grace perfects nature (ST I.1.8)
1154.hook: grace doesn't destroy nature but brings it to completion
1154.howItsDone: Catholic teachers often use Thomas's line that grace perfects nature to explain why the Church values reason, science, art and ordinary human gifts alongside faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the Summa works: objections, on the contrary, I answer that, and replies. Your line was state the other side first.

A piano tuner arrives at an old upright that hasn't been touched in years. She doesn't saw it in half or swap it for a synthesizer. She opens the lid, finds the strings and hammers already there, and works on them one by one, until it sounds the way it was built to sound. Same wood. Same keys. Only now, finished. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that works like that tuner. It's tucked into a reply early in the Summa, and it shapes how he holds faith and reason, God and the ordinary person. Today's word is that line.
screen: `AN OLD PIANO.` → `NOT SAWN IN HALF.` → `BROUGHT TO PITCH.`

segments.voice: It comes in the Summa's very first question, at the eighth article: does sacred teaching argue? Yes, Thomas says. Not to prove the faith, which rests on what God has revealed, but to start from it and make other things clear. Then an objection: if faith rests on God's word, doesn't bringing in human reason cheapen it? His reply, put plainly: grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it. So natural reason should serve faith, the way the will's natural leaning serves love. Nature is what a thing is made with. For a person: a mind that asks why, a body, a temperament, hands that can learn a craft. Grace is God's free gift. Thomas sets two pictures aside. In one, grace is a bulldozer: to be holy, stop being human. Flatten the mind, scorn the body. In the other, grace is a sticker, pasted on top, leaving you just as you were. Thomas's picture is the tuner: grace works on what's already there and brings it to completion. He shows it in the same reply. Paul, preaching in Athens, quotes the Greeks' own poets. In the Douay-Rheims, Acts gives his words: "as some also of your own poets said: For we are also his offspring." A pagan poet's line, put to work for the gospel. Reason wasn't thrown out. It was given a job. So Catholic teaching can say your curiosity, your humor, your patience with a tangled knot are not rivals to holiness. Catholics say grace takes them further than they could go alone.

Fresh snow, early morning, and a line of small prints crosses the yard, under the fence, and away. Nobody saw the fox. Tracks don't make themselves. You can know something passed, even its size and its hurry, without ever seeing its face. Now ask a question Thomas Aquinas asks near the start of the Summa. Can a person, thinking hard and honestly, get to God by reason? Or only by faith? Thomas's answer is neither of the easy ones. Today's word is the question itself.
screen: `PRINTS IN THE SNOW.` → `NOBODY SAW THE FOX.` → `CAN REASON GET TO GOD?`

segments.voice: Thomas takes it in steps. First: is God's existence obvious? In itself, yes, but not to us. His evidence is a psalm: the fool says in his heart, there is no God. If a person can think the opposite, it isn't obvious to us. Second: can it be shown, then? Yes, but only one way: from effects. We can't start from what God is, because we don't see that. We start from the world and reason back to its cause, the way you reason from tracks to the fox. Here he leans on Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Now the limits. Reason can reach that God is, not everything about God. Later in the Summa, Thomas says God being three persons, Father, Son and Spirit, is known by revelation, not by natural reason. And in the very first article he says something humbling: even the truths about God that reason can reach would be known only by a few, after a long time, with many errors mixed in. That's why, he says, God revealed them too. One more kindness. God's existence, Thomas says, isn't strictly an article of faith but something faith builds on, the way grace builds on nature. Yet a person who can't follow a proof may simply hold it by faith. No one is shut out for not being a philosopher. So the answer is yes, and. Reason can reach. It just doesn't reach the end of God.
screen: `OBVIOUS IN ITSELF, NOT TO US.` · `SHOWN FROM EFFECTS, LIKE TRACKS.` · `THAT GOD IS, NOT ALL GOD IS.` · `NO ONE SHUT OUT FOR LACK OF PROOFS.` · then, large: `BEING UNDERSTOOD BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.`
